Frozen fish releases liquid as it thaws in the basket. Pour it off at the halfway point rather than letting the fillet sit in it.

The 145°F debate, stated honestly

USDA guidance lists 145°F / 63°C for fish, and that is the rule this site follows. In professional kitchens, salmon is often pulled earlier, and many chefs argue that salmon is one of the few foods where the texture at 145°F is not what they want to serve.

That is a preference, not a safety standard, and it comes with a kitchen that knows its supplier and its handling. At home you cannot see the center, so the thermometer number stands. For anyone in a higher-risk group, cook to 145°F / 63°C.

Other fish and shellfish

The same rules apply, with two adjustments: thinner and leaner fish dry out faster, and shellfish turn rubbery in under a minute past done.

SeafoodTemperatureTimeNotes
Cod, 1 inch400°F / 205°C10–14 minCheck at 9 min
Tilapia, 1 inch390°F / 199°C9–12 minVery thin edges
Shrimp, raw, peeled390°F / 199°C6–9 minPink and opaque
Scallops, large, dry400°F / 205°C6–9 minPat bone dry first
Tuna steak, 1 inch400°F / 205°C6–10 minSame 145°F / 63°C rule

Five mistakes that ruin air fryer fish

  1. Cooking from the clock. Fish goes from done to dry in about 90 seconds.
  2. Wet fillets. Surface water steams the fish and stops the skin from crisping.
  3. Overcrowding. Leave space between pieces or the bottom steams instead of browning.
  4. High heat on a sugary glaze. Honey and maple burn before the center cooks.
  5. Forgetting the rest. Two minutes on the counter lets juices settle, though it does not replace the temperature check.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to flip salmon in an air fryer? Skin-on fillets do not need flipping. Steaks and thick skinless pieces benefit from one flip at the halfway point.

How long does salmon take at 400°F / 205°C? A one-inch fresh fillet takes roughly 7–10 min at that temperature, which is faster and less forgiving than 390°F / 199°C. Watch it closely the first time.

Can I cook salmon and vegetables together? Yes, if you give the vegetables a head start of about 5–8 minutes. Salmon finishes far sooner than potatoes or broccoli.

What does 145°F / 63°C salmon look like? Opaque all the way through, with flakes that separate when pressed with a fork. If the center is still glossy and translucent, it has not reached temperature.

The short version

Dry the fillet, oil it lightly, cook it skin side down in a single layer, and pull it at 145°F / 63°C. Everything else on this page is a refinement of those four steps.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Samosas: Frozen and Homemade Times
entry.summary: Air fryer samosa times for frozen and homemade pastries, with 380°F / 193°C settings, the cooked-filling rule and the oil spray that turns them gold.
entry.content:
Samosas are the pastry the air fryer handles better than deep frying: less oil, no splatter, and a wrapper that crisps around a spiced potato filling. The difference between crisp and pale is one preparation step — the oil spray — plus the cooked-filling rule.

This chart covers frozen and homemade samosas, the filling safety and the fixes.

Times vary by appliance model. Pastry thickness, filling moisture and basket crowding change the clock — watch the first batch.

Air fryer samosas chart

Frozen samosas go straight into the basket — no thawing. Thawing softens the pastry and it turns leathery instead of crisp.

SamosasTemperatureTimeNotes
Frozen, standard380°F / 193°C12–15 minFlip at halfway
Frozen, mini380°F / 193°C9–12 minShake once
Homemade, cooked filling380°F / 193°C10–12 minLight oil spray
Homemade, frozen on a tray380°F / 193°C12–15 minFreeze solid first
Spring roll wrappers, thinner380°F / 193°C8–10 minWatch closely

The oil spray is what turns homemade samosas golden: the pastry carries no fat, and a thin coat browns it evenly. Skip the spray and the wrapper toasts pale and dry.

The cooked-filling rule

The classic samosa filling — spiced potatoes and peas — is cooked before wrapping. The short air fryer cook browns the pastry; it is not long enough to cook raw vegetables or meat inside a wrapped pastry.

FillingThe rule
Potato and peaCook and cool before wrapping
Ground meatCook the meat to 160°F / 71°C before wrapping
PoultryCook the chicken to 165°F / 74°C before wrapping

Cool the filling completely before wrapping — hot filling steams the pastry from inside and softens it before the cook begins.

The homemade route

Samosa pastry (or spring roll wrappers as the shortcut) wraps around two tablespoons of filling, sealed with a flour paste. The flour-and-water paste holds through the cook; a dry seam opens and leaks.

StepTimeNotes
Cook and cool the filling20 minHot filling steams the pastry
Wrap, seal with flour paste3 minTwo tablespoons per samosa
Light oil spray—The step that turns them gold
Cook, flip at halfway10–12 minDeep gold, crisp
Freeze extras on a tray—Cook from frozen later

Freeze the shaped samosas on a tray until solid, then bag them — they cook from frozen at 12–15 minutes for months.

Five mistakes with air fryer samosas

  1. Thawing frozen samosas. Soft pastry turns leathery; cook them straight from frozen.
  2. Skipping the oil spray. The pastry carries no fat; a thin coat is what turns them gold.
  3. Hot filling in a fresh wrapper. Steam softens the pastry; cool the filling completely.
  4. Overfilling. Two tablespoons per samosa — stuffed pastries split and leak.
  5. Skipping the flip. The basket side stays pale; one turn at halfway keeps it even.

Frequently asked questions

How long do frozen samosas take in an air fryer? 12–15 minutes at 380°F / 193°C, flipped at halfway. Mini samosas need 9–12 minutes. No thawing and no oil needed.

Do samosas need oil in the air fryer? Frozen ones carry their own coating fat. Homemade ones need a light spray — the pastry has no fat and toasts pale without it.

Why are my samosas soggy? Hot filling, overfilling or a skipped flip. Cool the filling completely, use two tablespoons per pastry, and turn once at halfway.

Can I cook raw-meat fillings inside a samosa? No — the short cook browns the pastry but cannot cook raw meat inside. Cook the filling fully first: 160°F / 71°C for ground meat, 165°F / 74°C for poultry.

Can I freeze homemade samosas? Yes — freeze them on a tray until solid, then bag. They cook from frozen at 12–15 minutes and keep for months.

Samosas reward the same three habits every time: cooked-and-cooled filling, a light oil spray, one flip at halfway. The air fryer turns them crisp without any of the deep-fryer oil.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Sausage: Brats, Italian and Breakfast Times
entry.summary: Air fryer sausage times for fresh bratwurst and Italian links, smoked sausages and breakfast patties, with the internal temperatures to verify.
entry.content:
Sausages were born for hot air: the casing browns, the fat renders into the tray instead of the flame, and there is no flare-up to manage. But the sausage aisle mixes two very different products — raw links that must be cooked through, and fully cooked sausages that only need heating — and cooking them the same way ruins one of them.

This chart splits the two categories and gives times for each. Fresh sausage is ground pork, so under USDA rules it must reach 160°F / 71°C inside; fully cooked sausage just needs to be heated through.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage, basket size and link size change the clock, but the internal temperature rule does not change.

The two categories that matter

Read the package. The words "fully cooked", "smoked" or "heat and serve" mean the sausage is safe already and only needs browning. Anything labeled "raw" or "cook thoroughly" — most bratwurst, Italian links and breakfast patties — is ground meat and must be verified.

Sausage typeStatusTarget internal temperature
Fresh bratwurst, Italian, breakfast linksRaw160°F / 71°C
Breakfast sausage pattiesRaw160°F / 71°C
Smoked sausage, kielbasa, andouilleFully cookedHeat until steaming hot
Hot dogs and wienersFully cookedHeat until steaming hot

For raw links, probe the center of the thickest link at an angle, keeping the tip in the meat and away from the casing. Fully cooked sausages need no probe — heat them until the center is hot to the bite.

Air fryer sausage chart

Times assume a preheated basket and a single layer. Do not pierce the casings — the juices that keep the sausage juicy escape through every hole.

SausageTemperatureTimeNotes
Fresh bratwurst, raw380°F / 193°C12–15 minTurn at halfway, probe the center
Fresh Italian links, raw380°F / 193°C12–15 minTurn at halfway
Fresh breakfast links, thin380°F / 193°C8–10 minShake once
Breakfast patties, raw380°F / 193°C10–12 minFlip at halfway
Smoked sausage, fully cooked380°F / 193°C8–10 minBrowning only, turn once
Hot dogs, fully cooked390°F / 199°C4–6 minSplit lengthwise browns better

Fresh links benefit from a brief lower-temperature start — 3 minutes at 340°F / 170°C before raising to 380°F / 193°C — when the casings are thick and you want zero split skins. It is optional; the straight 380°F / 193°C cook is the standard.

Beer, onions and the rest of the bratwurst ritual

Traditional bratwurst is simmered in beer and onions before grilling. In the air fryer the par-simmer still works: poach the raw links gently in simmering beer or broth for 8–10 minutes, then brown them in the basket for 8–10 minutes at 380°F / 193°C. The poach keeps the interior juicy while the basket supplies the crust.

Skip the poach and simply extend the basket time to the long end of the range — 15 minutes — turning twice. Either route ends the same way: the thickest link probes 160°F / 71°C before it comes out.

Caramelized onions cook beautifully in the basket after the sausages come out: thin-sliced onions, a spoon of butter, 340°F / 170°C for 12–15 minutes with one stir at halfway.

Five mistakes with air fryer sausage

  1. Piercing the casing. Every fork hole drains the juices; tongs and a probe in the center instead.
  2. Cooking raw and smoked sausages the same. Raw needs the full time and a probe; smoked only needs browning.
  3. Stacking links in a second row. Overlap blocks the air and steams the covered casing.
  4. Maxing the heat for speed. Past 400°F / 205°C the casing splits and burns before the center cooks.
  5. Serving straight from the basket without checking. Fresh sausage must probe 160°F / 71°C, every batch.

Frequently asked questions

How long do bratwurst take in an air fryer? 12–15 minutes at 380°F / 193°C for raw brats, turned at halfway, until the center probes 160°F / 71°C. Fully cooked brats need only 8–10 minutes to brown.

Do I need to boil brats before air frying? No. A short beer or broth poach is optional and adds juiciness; the basket alone at the long end of the range does the job.

What temperature does sausage need inside? Fresh sausage is ground pork and must reach 160°F / 71°C under USDA rules. Fully cooked sausages have no raw center to worry about — heat them until steaming.

Why did my casings split? Heat too high or casings pierced. Keep the basket at 380°F / 193°C or below and handle the links with tongs, never a fork.

Can I cook frozen sausages in the air fryer? Fully cooked frozen sausages: yes, add 3–5 minutes to the browning time. Raw frozen links: thaw first, because the center must be verified and ice ruins the reading.

Two numbers carry this whole page: 160°F / 71°C for anything raw, and browning-only for anything fully cooked. Read the package, keep the layer single, and the air fryer turns out sausages better than any grill.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Shrimp: Times and Temperatures by Size and Type
entry.summary: Air fryer shrimp times by size for raw, frozen, shell-on, peeled and breaded shrimp, with why shrimp overcook in seconds and the 145°F / 63°C rule.
entry.content:
Shrimp is the fastest protein an air fryer cooks. It is also the least forgiving. A three-minute mistake turns sweet and springy into rubber, and no sauce fixes that.

So the chart below is a starting point and the thermometer is the decision. Work out what you have — raw or cooked, peeled or in the shell, fresh or frozen — because that changes the time more than any temperature setting does.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage and basket size change the clock, but 145°F / 63°C does not change.

Why shrimp go from done to rubber in seconds

A shrimp is thin. Most of it is less than half an inch from the surface, so heat reaches the center almost as fast as it reaches the outside. There is no thick core to buy you time, which is why the useful window is about 30 to 60 seconds.

The second reason is water. Shrimp are roughly three-quarters water, and as they heat that water squeezes out and the muscle fibers tighten. Past the safe temperature they keep tightening, and the texture turns firm, then chalky, then rubbery. Shrimp also carry enzymes that turn them mushy if they sit at a lukewarm temperature too long.

Shrimp are sold by count per pound, and the label is the size. U/15 means under 15 shrimp per pound, which is jumbo. 31/40 means 31 to 40 per pound, which is small. Buy by count, not by the word on the bag.

The rule: 145°F / 63°C, USDA

SeafoodSafe internal temperature
Shrimp, raw, all sizes and preparations145°F / 63°C
Shellfish generally, including shrimp145°F / 63°C
Cooked or reheated shrimp leftovers165°F / 74°C

Probe the thickest part of the thickest shrimp, entering from the back curve where the meat is deepest. On small shrimp the probe tip may be wider than the shrimp, so slide it in sideways along the body instead of stabbing straight down.

Shrimp have no rest-time allowance and no ground-meat exception. The number is the number.

Air fryer shrimp chart by size and preparation

Times assume a preheated basket, a single layer, and shrimp that are not touching.

ShrimpTemperatureTimeNotes
Small, 51/60 count, peeled390°F / 199°C4–6 minShake at 3 min, they finish fast
Medium, 31/40 count, peeled390°F / 199°C5–7 min145°F / 63°C
Large, 21/25 count, peeled390°F / 199°C6–8 minFlip once at halfway
Jumbo, U/15 count, peeled380°F / 193°C8–10 minCheck at 7 min
Colossal, U/10 count380°F / 193°C9–12 minLower heat, thicker body
Any size, tail-on, shell split390°F / 199°C6–9 minTail slows the thick end
Any size, shell-on, whole380°F / 193°C7–11 minShell insulates slightly
Raw, frozen, peeled380°F / 193°C9–13 minAdd 3–4 min to thawed time
Breaded, frozen, pre-cooked400°F / 205°C8–11 minFollow package directions
Skewered, packed lightly390°F / 199°C7–9 minLeave gaps between shrimp

Small shrimp can go from translucent to overcooked before you finish setting the timer. Stand at the machine for the last two minutes of any batch under seven minutes.

Peeled or shell-on: what the shell actually does

Peeled shrimp cook faster and take on seasoning and marinade directly. They also dry out faster, because the shell is a layer of protection that peeled shrimp no longer have. Olive oil, butter or a marinade is not optional here.

Shell-on shrimp take two to three minutes longer and stay juicier, and the shell carries flavor that the meat picks up while it cooks. Split the shell down the back with scissors and devein, but leave it on. Eat them with your fingers, or peel them at the table.

Tail-on is a third case. The tail is the last part to cook and the first part to burn if it touches the element, so lay tails toward the middle of the basket.

Raw, frozen and cooked shrimp are three different jobs

Raw fresh shrimp from the counter: pat dry, oil lightly, season, cook 5–10 minutes depending on size, and pull them at 145°F / 63°C.

Raw frozen shrimp need no thawing if they are individually frozen and loose, but add three to four minutes and expect water in the basket. Pour it off at the halfway point so the shrimp brown instead of steam. If they are frozen into a solid block, thaw them in the refrigerator overnight first, because a block will not cook evenly.

Pre-cooked shrimp, the pink kind sold at the fish counter: they are already cooked, and they only need reheating. Give them 3–5 minutes at 350°F / 177°C, just until hot. Reheated leftovers are a 165°F / 74°C job, not 145°F / 63°C, because cooked seafood that has been stored and rewarmed is held to the higher reheating standard.

Breaded shrimp and the oil question

Frozen breaded shrimp — popcorn, butterfly, coconut, panko — go in straight from the freezer at 400°F / 205°C and need no added oil. The coating is already designed to crisp, and oil makes it greasy and soft.

Breaded shrimp also hide the meat, so you cannot see doneness through the coating. If the package says the product is raw, it must reach 165°F / 74°C in the center, because that is the standard for any reheated or previously cooked food. If the package says it is fully cooked and you are only heating it, follow the package directions and heat it through.

For homemade breading, press the crumbs on with a dry hand, chill for 15 minutes, and cook at 400°F / 205°C for 7–10 minutes, turning once. Chilling keeps the coating on instead of in the basket.

Five mistakes with air fryer shrimp

  1. Walking away. Four to eight minutes is not enough time to leave the kitchen.
  2. Overcrowding. Stacked shrimp steam, and the ones underneath never get crisp.
  3. Skipping the oil on peeled shrimp. They need a light coating or they dry out.
  4. Thawing under warm water. It starts cooking the outside before the inside is thawed.
  5. Marinating for hours. Acid in a marinade turns shrimp mushy. Twenty to thirty minutes is plenty.

Frequently asked questions

How long do shrimp take in an air fryer?

Four to six minutes for small peeled shrimp at 390°F / 199°C, and eight to ten minutes for jumbo at 380°F / 193°C. Check the thickest one with a thermometer and pull them at 145°F / 63°C.

Can I put frozen shrimp straight in the air fryer?

Yes, if they are individually frozen and loose. Add three to four minutes to the thawed time and pour off the water at the halfway point.

Is 145°F / 63°C enough for shrimp?

Yes. USDA sets 145°F / 63°C for fish and shellfish. Shrimp served cold in a shrimp cocktail are cooked to the same target, then chilled quickly.

Do I need to devein shrimp?

It is a texture preference, not a safety step. The dark vein along the back is digestive tract, and most people remove it for appearance. If you leave it, the shrimp is still safe at 145°F / 63°C.

Can I cook shrimp and vegetables together?

Only if the vegetables get a head start. Shrimp finish in four to ten minutes, while peppers or broccoli need ten to fifteen. Cook the vegetables first, then add the shrimp for the last few minutes.

The short version

Dry them, oil the peeled ones, single layer, 390°F / 199°C for small and medium, 380°F / 193°C for jumbo, and check at the early end of the range. Pull them at 145°F / 63°C, and serve them the moment they come out of the basket.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Steak: Times, Temperatures and the 3-Minute Rest Rule
entry.summary: Air fryer steak times by thickness, doneness temperatures from rare to well done, flipping and preheating, and the 145°F / 63°C plus 3-minute rest rule.
entry.content:
An air fryer will not give you a steakhouse crust. What it will give you is a steak cooked evenly through in about the time it takes to set a table, with no pan to deglaze and no smoke alarm. The trade is honest: convenience and consistency, in exchange for the hard sear a cast iron pan produces.

The rule: 145°F / 63°C, then rest 3 minutes

USDA guidance for whole cuts of beef is 145°F / 63°C with a 3-minute rest. The rest is part of the standard, because the temperature holds and the juices redistribute while the meat sits.

Cut typeSafe internal temperature
Whole cuts of beef, pork, veal (steaks, chops, roasts)145°F / 63°C + 3 min rest
Ground beef, including burger patties160°F / 71°C
Reheated steak leftovers165°F / 74°C

That distinction matters more than anything else on this page. A whole steak can safely be served medium-rare. Ground beef cannot. Once beef is ground, surface bacteria are mixed through the interior, so the middle of a burger has to reach 160°F / 71°C no matter how it is cooked or who is asking. There is no medium-rare burger that is safe by the same standard as a medium-rare steak.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer, not the clock. Air fryer models differ in wattage, basket size and how close the element sits to the food, so every time below is a range. Finish with an instant-read thermometer, inserted into the thickest part and away from bone and fat. Cook to 145°F / 63°C or above for anyone in a higher-risk group: young children, pregnant people, older adults, and anyone with a weakened immune system.

Why 1 inch and 1.5 inches are not the same steak

A one-inch steak and a one-and-a-half-inch steak differ by fifty percent in thickness, and that is closer to a hundred percent more time. The outer half-inch on each side cooks fast because the moving air hits it directly, while the center warms by conduction from the outside in.

So a one-inch steak can hit medium-rare in ten minutes while one-and-a-half inches needs fifteen to twenty. Cook both on one timer and you get one good steak and one overcooked one. Measure the thickness before you set the temperature.

ThicknessTemperatureTimeDoneness if you follow itNotes
3/4 inch400°F / 205°C6–9 minRare to medium-rareFlip at halfway
1 inch400°F / 205°C9–13 minMedium-rareCheck at 8 min
1.25 inches390°F / 199°C11–15 minMedium-rareFlip once
1.5 inches380°F / 193°C14–19 minMedium-rareCheck at 12 min
2 inches375°F / 190°C18–24 minMedium-rareRest 5 min, not 3

Thicker steaks want lower heat and more time. High heat on a two-inch steak blackens the outside while the center stays cool.

Doneness temperatures

Pull the steak a few degrees below your target and let the rest carry it the last bit.

DonenessTarget temperatureNotes
Rare120–125°F / 49–52°CBelow USDA minimum
Medium-rare130–135°F / 54–57°CBelow USDA minimum
Medium140–145°F / 60–63°CAt the USDA minimum
Medium-well150–155°F / 66–68°CAbove the minimum
Well done160°F / 71°C and aboveDry without careful timing

Here is the honest part. The USDA figure of 145°F / 63°C is a minimum for safety, not a recommendation for flavor. Everything under it is a deliberate trade that some people make and others do not. Serve 145°F / 63°C or above to anyone in a higher-risk group, as listed in the warning above.

Preheat and flip: the two things that decide the outcome

Preheat. Three to five minutes at the cooking temperature, empty. A cold basket dries the surface before it browns, which is how you get gray steak.

Flip once. One flip at the halfway point is right for nearly every thickness. Flipping repeatedly cools the surface and slows browning.

Dry the surface. Pat the steak dry and oil the meat, not the basket.

Five mistakes that ruin air fryer steak

  1. Cooking to time instead of temperature. Thickness beats every chart, including this one.
  2. Skipping the rest. Cutting at once loses the juice onto the plate.
  3. Overcrowding. Two steaks need two batches or a bigger basket.
  4. Going straight from the fridge. Twenty minutes on the counter gives a more even cook.
  5. Expecting a crust. Use a grill pan for thirty seconds per side afterward if you want one.

Frequently asked questions

Can I cook a frozen steak in an air fryer? It works, but unevenly. Add roughly 8–12 minutes to the times above and check the temperature early and often. Thawing first is better.

Do I need to rest the steak for exactly 3 minutes? Three minutes is the USDA rest that goes with 145°F / 63°C. Five minutes is better for steaks an inch and a half or thicker.

What temperature for a medium-rare air fryer steak? Set the appliance to 400°F / 205°C for a one-inch steak and pull it at 130–135°F / 54–57°C, understanding that this sits below the USDA minimum of 145°F / 63°C.

Can I cook steak and vegetables together? Give the vegetables a 5–8 minute head start, and keep them in a single layer so the steak still gets direct air.

The short version

Measure the thickness, preheat, oil the steak, flip once at halfway, and pull it at your target temperature with a thermometer. Rest it three minutes. That is the whole method.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Temperature Guide: When to Use 320, 350, 375 or 400
entry.summary: What each air fryer temperature is for, from 320°F / 160°C for delicate foods to 400°F / 205°C for crisping, with adjustments for frozen food.
entry.content:
Most air fryer confusion is temperature confusion. The machine can hold anything from 180°F / 82°C to 400°F / 205°C, and the difference between perfect and disappointing is usually just picking the right rung on that ladder — then leaving the food alone long enough.

This guide maps the common settings to the jobs they do best, explains why frozen food and fresh food rarely use the same number, and covers the adjustments that recipes assume you already know.

Times vary by appliance model. Wattage changes how fast a setting reaches the food, so use times as starting points and verify doneness the usual way.

What the air fryer actually does with temperature

An air fryer is a compact convection oven: a heating element and a fan that pushes hot air around a small space. Because the chamber is small, the air moves fast and transfers heat more aggressively than a conventional oven at the same dial setting. That is why air fryer temperatures run 25°F / 14°C to 50°F / 28°C lower than the oven temperatures printed on frozen food bags.

The practical rule: when converting an oven recipe, subtract 25°F / 14°C and check for doneness about 20 percent earlier.

The temperature ladder

SettingBest forExamples
320°F / 160°CDelicate foods, melting, dehydratingCheese melts, reheating pizza, dried fruit
340°F / 170°CGentle browning, glazes, vegetables that burn easilyOnions, sugary marinades
350°F / 177°CEven roasting, dense items, whole proteinsWhole chicken, meatloaf, thick bread
375°F / 190°CThe all-rounder for proteinsChicken breast, pork chops
380°F / 193°CStandard crisping with fat to renderThighs, wings, sausages
390°F / 199°CFaster crisping, thicker coatingsFrozen breaded foods
400°F / 205°CMaximum crisping, finishing, thin foodsFries, bacon, crisp finishes

Two settings anchor everything. Roasting dense food that must cook through uses moderate heat, 350°F / 177°C to 380°F / 193°C, so the center catches up before the surface burns. Crisping food that is already safe to eat — fries, frozen snacks, bacon — uses 400°F / 205°C, where speed and surface texture are the whole point.

Frozen versus fresh: why the numbers differ

Frozen food usually wants a hotter setting than the same food fresh. The food starts cold in the middle, so the extra heat compensates while the coating still crisps.

FoodFreshFrozen
Chicken wings380°F / 193°C380°F / 193°C, longer time
Breaded chicken375°F / 190°C390°F / 199°C
French fries, from raw potato380°F / 193°C400°F / 205°C (bag instructions)
Fish fillets, breaded380°F / 193°C390°F / 199°C

The pattern to remember: freezing changes the clock more than the temperature, except for thin breaded items, where the coating benefits from the extra heat. Raw proteins are the exception to every shortcut here — thaw them first, because a frozen center makes doneness impossible to verify.

Preheating, shaking and other multipliers

The dial is only one of three controls. The other two change results as much:

  • Preheating, 3 minutes. Food that starts in a hot basket browns sooner and sticks less. Most important for proteins and anything with a coating.
  • Shaking or flipping. Moving the food exposes new surfaces. Fries and small items want a shake every 5 to 8 minutes; larger cuts want one flip at halfway.
  • Basked density. A half-full basket cooks like the chart; a packed one needs longer and never crisps properly. Single layer is the rule the chart times assume.

Oil is the fourth variable, but it is forgiving: a light spray improves browning on most fresh foods, while pre-coated frozen food needs none.

When to lower the temperature instead of raising it

Counterintuitively, most air fryer failures come from too much heat, not too little:

  • Burnt outside, cold inside. Drop 20°F / 11°C and add time; the heat needs to reach the center.
  • Sugary sauces turning black. Glaze in the last few minutes at a moderate setting.
  • Lean meat turning dry. Lower heat with a thermometer check beats high heat with a timer.
  • Cheese scorching on melts. Cover loosely with foil for the first half of the cook.

High heat is a finishing tool, not a cooking strategy. Cook through at a moderate setting, then raise the temperature for the last few minutes if you want extra color.

Five mistakes with air fryer temperatures

  1. Following the oven temperature on a bag. Subtract 25°F / 14°C or the outside burns first.
  2. Using maximum heat for everything. 400°F / 205°C is for crisping, not for cooking through.
  3. Changing two variables at once. Adjust temperature or time, never both in the same batch.
  4. Skipping preheat for proteins. A cold start adds minutes unevenly and ruins timing.
  5. Trusting one machine's numbers blindly. Two models at the same setting can differ by 15°F / 8°C; learn yours.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best all-purpose air fryer temperature? 375°F / 190°C to 380°F / 193°C covers most proteins and vegetables. If you only memorize one setting, make it 380°F / 193°C and adjust the time.

Why do frozen food instructions say to use a lower oven temperature? They are written for still ovens. The air fryer's fast-moving air needs 25°F / 14°C less to deliver the same heat, and it cooks faster too.

Can I use 400°F / 205°C for raw chicken? Not for the whole cook. Thin pieces might survive it, but on anything thick the surface scorches before the center is done. Cook at a moderate setting and finish hot if needed.

Does a bigger air fryer need different temperatures? Larger chambers move more air over more food, so times stretch slightly and the temperature stays the same. Expect a few extra minutes versus the smallest baskets.

How do I know my machine runs hot or cool? Watch the first few batches: consistent early browning means it runs hot, pale results that take longer than charts predict mean it runs cool. Adjust by 15°F / 8°C and note it.

Temperature is the steering wheel of the air fryer. Choose the rung that matches the food's density, verify doneness independently of the clock, and the same machine will handle delicate melts and hard crisps with equal confidence.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Tofu: Crispy Cubes, Times and Temperatures
entry.summary: Air fryer tofu times and temperatures by cube size, plus pressing, firm versus extra-firm versus silken tofu, cornstarch coating and a crispiness fix.
entry.content:
Tofu is the one air fryer food where preparation decides everything. A wet, bare block comes out pale, soft, and stuck to the plate. The same block, pressed and dusted with cornstarch, comes out with a shell you can hear when you bite it.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for the numbers that matter, and treat every time below as a range. Wattage and basket size can move the clock by several minutes.

Tofu is ready to eat, so there is no USDA minimum temperature

This is the honest version. USDA publishes safe minimum internal temperatures for meat, poultry, fish and egg dishes. It does not publish one for tofu, because tofu is not a raw animal product and does not need to reach a safety temperature to be eaten. So there is no tofu temperature to hit, and this chart will not invent one. The temperatures below are cooking settings for browning and texture; the numbers that matter here are about storage and reheating.

Tofu safety pointGuidance
Refrigerate cooked tofu within2 hours
Eat cooked tofu within3–4 days
Reheated tofu leftovers165°F / 74°C
A raw block from the fridgeReady to eat, no cooking needed

Firm, extra-firm and silken: only two of these work

Tofu is sold by water content, and water is the enemy of crispness.

Tofu typeWaterAir fryer resultVerdict
SilkenVery highSteams inside, never browns, falls apartSkip it
SoftHighBreaks apart when tossedSkip it
FirmMediumBrowns, soft center, needs longer pressingWorks
Extra-firmLowCrisp edges, holds its shapeBest choice
Super-firm or pressedLowestVery crisp, almost chewyWorks, watch the time

Silken tofu fails for a physical reason. It is set with less coagulant and holds far more water, so in hot moving air that water turns to steam inside the cube. The surface never stays dry long enough to brown. Silken belongs in soup; firm and extra-firm are the ones that crisp.

Pressing: fifteen minutes minimum

Wrap the block in a clean towel, set it on a plate, and put a heavy pan or a couple of cans on top for 15–30 minutes. That removes the water that would otherwise steam the cube from the inside.

Short on time? Cut the block into cubes first, spread them on a towel, and press a second towel over them for 10 minutes. Salt after pressing, not before: salt early draws out more water and leaves the surface damp.

Cornstarch: the coating that makes the crust

Dust, do not dredge. One tablespoon of cornstarch for a 14–16 oz block, tossed until every face has a thin coat, then shake off the excess. A thick layer turns gummy and tastes of raw starch.

A teaspoon of oil in the bowl helps the coating stick and brown. Skip wet batter: it drips and can burn onto the element.

Cube size chart: temperature and time

Times assume a preheated basket, a single layer, and a 14–16 oz block. Shake at the halfway mark unless the notes say otherwise.

Cube sizeTemperatureTimeNotes
1/2 inch400°F / 205°C10–13 minCrisp through, best for grain bowls
3/4 inch390°F / 199°C12–15 minThe all-purpose size
1 inch380°F / 193°C14–18 minSoft center, good for skewers
Triangles, 1/4 inch thick375°F / 190°C12–16 minMore surface, very crisp
Torn chunks, 1.5 inch380°F / 193°C16–20 minRagged edges brown fastest

Flipping: shake, do not fuss

A single layer is worth more than any amount of flipping. When cubes touch, those faces stay pale.

Shake the basket every 5–6 minutes for half-inch and three-quarter-inch cubes, and roll triangles and one-inch cubes with tongs once at halfway. Do not open the basket constantly; the temperature drops every time.

Troubleshooting crispiness

ProblemLikely causeFix
Pale, soft cubesNot pressed, or coated while wetPress 30 min, pat dry, dust again
Gummy coatingToo much cornstarchOne thin dust, shake off the excess
Dark edges, soft centerTemperature too high for the sizeDrop to 380°F / 193°C, add 3–4 min
Sticking to the basketCold basket, no oil on the tofuPreheat 3 min, oil the tofu lightly

Five mistakes with air fryer tofu

  1. Skipping the press. Wet tofu steams instead of browning, and no setting fixes that.
  2. Buying silken for a crisp recipe. It cannot hold its shape in moving air.
  3. Crowding the basket. Two layers cook unevenly and the middle stays soft.
  4. Saucing too early. A wet sauce softens the crust you just built.
  5. Expecting deep-fried crunch with no oil. A light oil toss gets close; none at all gets dry.

Frequently asked questions

What temperature do I cook tofu in an air fryer? Between 380°F / 193°C and 400°F / 205°C for most cubes. Half-inch cubes take the higher setting; one-inch cubes brown more evenly at the lower one.

How long does tofu take in an air fryer? 10–13 minutes for half-inch cubes and 14–18 minutes for one-inch cubes, shaken at halfway.

Is reheated tofu safe? Yes. Reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C, the USDA figure for reheated food, and eat cooked tofu within 3–4 days.

The short version

Press, cut evenly, dust with cornstarch, oil lightly, preheat, and cook in a single layer at 380°F / 193°C to 400°F / 205°C for 10–18 minutes depending on size. Shake at halfway and sauce after the basket comes out. There is no internal temperature to hit.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Turkey Breast: Times by Weight for Bone-In and Boneless
entry.summary: Air fryer turkey breast times by weight for bone-in, boneless, fresh and frozen, with brining, the 165°F / 74°C rule and why a whole turkey will not fit.
entry.content:
A turkey breast is the sensible answer to a holiday bird in an air fryer. It is small enough to fit, it cooks in about an hour, and it is almost all white meat, which is the part everyone reaches for first.

A whole turkey is not an option in a normal air fryer, and that is a size fact rather than a technique problem. Below are the weights that do fit, the times they need, and the fix for a whole bird.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage and basket size change the clock, but 165°F / 74°C does not change.

The rule: 165°F / 74°C for all poultry

PoultrySafe internal temperature
Turkey breast, bone-in or boneless165°F / 74°C
Ground turkey and turkey sausage165°F / 74°C
Reheated turkey leftovers165°F / 74°C

USDA sets one number for poultry, and it does not change for white meat, dark meat, ground turkey or a reheated plate. There is no medium-rare turkey and no pink center that is safe by a lower standard.

Probe the thickest part of the breast, away from the bone. Bone conducts heat differently and reads high, so a probe touching bone can tell you the turkey is done when the meat around it is not. If you are cooking a stuffed breast, the stuffing must also reach 165°F / 74°C.

Air fryer turkey breast chart by weight

Times assume a preheated basket, a breast at room temperature for 20 minutes before cooking, and space around it for air to move.

Turkey breastTemperatureTimeNotes
Boneless roast, 2 lb360°F / 182°C30–40 minCheck at 28 min
Boneless roast, 3 lb350°F / 177°C40–50 minRest 10 min before slicing
Boneless roast, 4 lb350°F / 177°C50–60 minLargest that fits most baskets
Bone-in half breast, 2–3 lb350°F / 177°C40–50 minProbe away from bone
Bone-in half breast, 4–5 lb340°F / 171°C55–70 minCheck at 50 min
Bone-in half breast, 6 lb330°F / 166°C70–85 minNeeds a large basket
Turkey tenderloin, 1 lb375°F / 190°C20–25 minFast, lean, easy to dry
Cutlets, 0.5 inch380°F / 193°C10–14 minFlip at halfway
Frozen boneless roast, 3 lb340°F / 171°C75–95 minOnly if labeled cook from frozen

Bone-in takes longer per pound than boneless because the bone blocks heat and adds mass that has to come up to temperature. A six-pound bone-in half breast is close to the limit of what most five- to six-quart baskets will hold, and it needs a lower temperature so the outside does not dry before the center is done.

For a boneless roast, tie it if it is loose so the thickness is even. An uneven roast finishes at the thin end long before the thick middle, and by the time the middle reads 165°F / 74°C the thin end is sliced meat for sandwiches.

Brining, and why it is worth the time

Turkey breast is lean white meat with little fat to protect it, and the air fryer moves hot air across the surface constantly. A wet brine adds water and seasoning, and it is the single biggest improvement you can make to the result.

For a simple brine, dissolve one-half cup of kosher salt and one-quarter cup of sugar in one gallon of cold water. Submerge the breast and refrigerate for four to twelve hours. Rinse it, pat it completely dry, and let it sit uncovered in the refrigerator for an hour so the skin dries. Dry skin browns; wet skin steams.

Do not brine a turkey breast that is already enhanced, injected or self-basting. Read the label, because those products have salt and water added and brining them makes the meat salty rather than juicy.

A dry brine works too: rub the breast with salt and leave it uncovered in the refrigerator overnight. It seasons the meat and dries the surface with less counter space.

Why a whole turkey does not fit

A whole turkey needs a cavity of hot air around it, not just a basket big enough to hold it. In a round or square air fryer basket the bird touches the sides and the element guard, and the air cannot circulate around it. The outside overcooks while the center stays cold, and the top skin can scorch against the heating element.

Two workable answers exist. The first is a turkey breast, which is what this page is about. The second is spatchcocking: remove the backbone with kitchen shears, press the bird flat, and cook it in two halves or in a large single layer.

A spatchcocked turkey that has been flattened to a fairly even thickness cooks in roughly 80–110 minutes at 330–350°F / 166–177°C in a large air fryer or a countertop oven with an air fry setting. Flattening is what makes it possible: even thickness means the breast and the thighs can reach 165°F / 74°C at close to the same time. Even then, check the bird against the element guard before you close the basket, and cook it in two batches if it does not clear.

A short note for Thanksgiving and Christmas

Holiday cooking in an air fryer means one bird at a time and a plan for the oven. A four- pound boneless breast takes about 45–60 minutes from a preheated basket, which is faster than a full-size oven and frees the oven for sides. Cook it early, tent it with foil, and hold it at a safe hot temperature rather than letting it sit out on the counter. Reheat any leftover turkey to 165°F / 74°C.

If your gathering needs a whole bird for the table, spatchcock it in the oven and use the air fryer for a second breast. Two smaller pieces of meat cook more predictably than one large one.

Five mistakes with air fryer turkey breast

  1. Probing the bone. Bone reads high, so you stop cooking too early.
  2. Cooking it cold from the refrigerator. Let it sit out 20 minutes so the center is not fighting the clock.
  3. Crowding the basket. The breast needs air on all sides, or the bottom steams.
  4. Slicing immediately. Rest 10–15 minutes so the juices redistribute instead of running onto the board.
  5. Reheating at high heat. Use a lower temperature until hot, and reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a turkey breast take in an air fryer?

A three-pound boneless roast takes 40–50 minutes at 350°F / 177°C. A four- to five-pound bone-in half breast takes 55–70 minutes at 340°F / 171°C. Always finish by probing the thickest part for 165°F / 74°C.

Bone-in or boneless for an air fryer?

Boneless is easier: it cooks faster, fits smaller baskets and slices cleanly. Bone-in has more flavor and stays juicier, but it needs a lower temperature, more time and a larger basket.

Can I cook a frozen turkey breast in an air fryer?

Only if the label says it is formulated to cook from frozen. Otherwise thaw it in the refrigerator, which takes about 24 hours for a three- to four-pound breast. A raw frozen breast cooks unevenly and is hard to verify with a thermometer.

Can I cook a whole turkey in an air fryer?

Not a standard 12- to 20-pound bird. There is no room for air to circulate and the top touches the element. Spatchcock the turkey instead, or cook a breast and reserve the oven for the rest.

Do I need to baste a turkey breast in the air fryer?

No. Opening the basket drops the temperature and the moving air already browns the surface. If the skin is browning too fast, tent it loosely with foil and lower the temperature.

The short version

Choose a boneless roast of three to four pounds or a bone-in half breast of four to five, brine it if you have time, dry the skin, and cook it at 340–350°F / 171–177°C for 40–70 minutes depending on the cut. Rest it for 10–15 minutes, and probe the thickest part for 165°F / 74°C before it goes to the table.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Turkey Burgers: Juicy Patties at the Right Temperature
entry.summary: Air fryer turkey burger times for fresh and frozen patties, with 375°F / 190°C settings and the 165°F / 74°C internal rule for ground turkey.
entry.content:
Turkey burgers are leaner than beef, which makes them faster to cook and easier to dry. The air fryer helps — hot air browns the outside while the fat that renders stays with the patty — but the narrow window between juicy and sawdust means the thermometer decides.

This chart covers fresh and frozen patties. Ground turkey must reach 165°F / 74°C inside under USDA rules — there is no thickness or seasoning that changes it.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage, basket size and patty thickness change the clock, but 165°F / 74°C does not change.

The rule for ground turkey

Ground turkey mixes the surface into the center, so the center must be cooked through:

Ground turkeySafe internal temperature
Fresh patties, any thickness165°F / 74°C
Frozen patties, cooked from frozen165°F / 74°C
Turkey burgers, reheated165°F / 74°C

Probe the center of the patty from the side, horizontally, so the tip sits in the middle of the meat. A vertical probe can push through the thin bottom and read hot basket air instead.

Air fryer turkey burger chart

Times assume a preheated basket, even thickness and a single layer. Turkey is leaner than beef, so a light coating of oil on the patty keeps the surface from drying as it browns.

PattyTemperatureTimeNotes
Fresh, 1/4 lb, 1/2 inch375°F / 190°C10–12 minFlip at halfway
Fresh, 1/3 lb, 3/4 inch375°F / 190°C12–16 minFlip once, check early
Fresh, 1/2 lb, 1 inch375°F / 190°C15–18 minDimple the center
Frozen, 1/4 lb375°F / 190°C14–17 minFlip at halfway
Frozen, 1/3 lb375°F / 190°C16–20 minVerify the center carefully

Frozen patties frequently need the long end of their range — the center thaws as it cooks, so verify the middle before building the burger.

Keeping lean turkey juicy

Lean meat dries faster than fatty meat, and turkey at 93/7 is much leaner than beef at 80/20. Four habits close the gap:

  • A little fat in the mix. A tablespoon of olive oil or finely chopped bacon per pound of meat restores moisture the lean grind lacks.
  • Gentle mixing. Compact patties turn dense; mix just until the seasoning spreads.
  • Do not press during cooking. Pressing squeezes out the juices that keep the patty moist.
  • Pull at temperature, not past it. The moment the thermometer reads 165°F / 74°C, the patty is done — every extra minute dries lean turkey visibly.

Binders also help: two tablespoons of bread crumbs soaked in milk per pound keep the crumb soft. Too much binder turns the patty dense, so stay light.

Five mistakes with air fryer turkey burgers

  1. Judging by the crust. Golden browning hides a raw center; probe the middle every time.
  2. Skipping the oil coat. Lean turkey dries on the surface without a thin coat of fat.
  3. Pressing patties during cooking. Pressing drains the moisture the lean meat needs.
  4. Cooking straight from the fridge. Cold centers lag; rest patties 15 minutes for even timing.
  5. Overcooking past 165°F / 74°C. Lean turkey has no fat reserve; pull at temperature.

Frequently asked questions

How long do turkey burgers take in an air fryer? 10–12 minutes at 375°F / 190°C for fresh quarter-pound patties, 12–16 minutes for third-pound, and 14–20 minutes for frozen. Verify the center reaches 165°F / 74°C.

What temperature do turkey burgers need inside? 165°F / 74°C — the USDA minimum for all ground turkey, fresh or frozen. Use an instant-read thermometer through the side of the patty.

Why are my turkey burgers dry? The cook ran past temperature or the patty had no fat reserve. Pull at 165°F / 74°C promptly, add a tablespoon of oil per pound to the mix, and skip the press.

Can I cook frozen turkey patties without thawing? Yes — 14–20 minutes at 375°F / 190°C, flipped at halfway. Verify the center; frozen patties often need the long end.

Do turkey burgers smoke in an air fryer? Less than beef — turkey renders less fat. Keep the temperature at or below 375°F / 190°C and wipe the drawer between batches.

Turkey burgers reward precision: even patties with a dimple, 375°F / 190°C, a flip at halfway, and 165°F / 74°C in the middle — pulled the moment the thermometer agrees.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Vegetables Chart (Fresh and Frozen Times)
entry.summary: Printable air fryer vegetables chart for fresh and frozen vegetables, with the 1 tsp per cup oil rule, times, temperatures and crispiness fixes.
entry.content:
Vegetables are where an air fryer surprises people. The same machine that rescues frozen fries turns broccoli into something with browned edges and a little chew, in under 10 minutes and without heating the kitchen.

They are also where people give up fastest, because a dry vegetable in hot moving air does not roast. It dehydrates, then scorches at the tips.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for meat, and your eyes and a fork for vegetables.

The oil rule: about 1 teaspoon per cup

This is the single change that fixes most disappointing air fryer vegetables. Use roughly 1 tsp of oil per cup of cut vegetables — about 1 tbsp for a 4-cup basket — and toss until every piece has a faint sheen. No pools in the bottom of the bowl, no dry patches.

Oil does two jobs here. It carries heat across the surface so the vegetable browns instead of drying, and it holds any seasoning you add. Vegetables with a dry surface burn at the thin edges while the middle stays raw.

Two more rules matter as much as the oil:

  • Cut evenly. A 1-inch piece and a 2-inch piece of the same carrot cannot finish together.
  • Stay in one layer. Two layers of vegetables steam. Steamed vegetables are soft and pale, and more time will not fix that.

Air fryer fresh vegetables chart

Every time below assumes one layer, cut pieces of similar size, and a basket preheated for about 3 minutes.

VegetableTemperatureTimeNotes
Broccoli florets380°F / 193°C8–10 minDry well before oiling
Cauliflower florets390°F / 199°C12–15 minShake at 8 min
Brussels sprouts, halved390°F / 199°C15–18 minCut side down first
Bell peppers, 1-inch pieces380°F / 193°C10–12 minShake once
Zucchini, half moons380°F / 193°C10–12 minSalt after, not before
Green beans380°F / 193°C8–10 minTrim the ends
Asparagus390°F / 199°C7–9 minThin spears cook fast
Carrots, 1-inch chunks380°F / 193°C15–18 minToss well in oil
Sweet potato cubes400°F / 205°C15–18 minShake twice
Potato wedges400°F / 205°C18–22 minSoak 10 min, then dry
Red onion wedges390°F / 199°C12–15 minSeparate the layers
Butternut squash cubes400°F / 205°C16–20 minCut to 1 inch or less
Mushrooms, halved380°F / 193°C10–12 minDo not salt early
Cherry tomatoes380°F / 193°C6–8 minThey will burst
Corn on the cob, halved390°F / 199°C12–15 minBrush with oil

Salting early is a real mistake for zucchini, mushrooms and tomatoes. Salt pulls water to the surface, and that water steams the vegetable instead of browning it. Season after.

Air fryer frozen vegetables chart

Frozen vegetables are already blanched, so they need less time than raw and they will never be as crisp. The trade is worth it on a weeknight. Do not thaw them first — thawed frozen vegetables release water and turn limp.

Frozen vegetableTemperatureTimeNotes
Mixed vegetables390°F / 199°C10–14 minShake at halfway
Broccoli florets390°F / 199°C10–13 minShake twice
Green beans390°F / 199°C10–12 minPat off ice crystals
Peas350°F / 177°C8–10 minShake once
Corn kernels380°F / 193°C8–10 minShake once
Butternut squash cubes400°F / 205°C15–18 minShake twice
Cauliflower rice380°F / 193°C8–12 minShake every 4 min

Shake frozen vegetables more often than fresh ones. They start as a solid block, and the pieces that stay pressed together stay wet.

Vegetables that do not work in an air fryer

Two families fail, and it is worth knowing which before you waste a batch.

Leafy greens. Spinach, kale, arugula and lettuce are too light and too thin. The fan lifts them into the heating element, where they burn in seconds, and long before that they wither to almost nothing. Use a skillet, or roast them in a sheet pan you can watch.

Battered items. Tempura, beer-battered cauliflower and anything with a wet batter will slide off and pool in the basket. The batter needs oil to set. Frozen breaded vegetables are different — those are pre-fried and work well.

Also skip anything you want fully soft and wet, like a stewed tomato dish. An air fryer removes moisture; that is its whole personality.

Five mistakes that keep vegetables from crisping

  1. Too little oil. Under 1 tsp per cup and the surface dries before it browns.
  2. Wet vegetables. Water on the surface turns to steam. Dry them on a towel first.
  3. A crowded basket. One layer, or cook in two batches.
  4. No shake. Anything in more than a single loose layer needs a shake at halfway.
  5. Salting at the start. Salt draws water out. Add it when the vegetables come out.

Frequently asked questions

Should I preheat the air fryer for vegetables? Yes, about 3 minutes at the cooking temperature. A cold basket gives you pale, soft vegetables even if the time is right.

Why are my vegetables burnt outside and raw inside? The pieces are too big or uneven, or the temperature is too high for the thickness. Cut smaller, drop to 380°F / 193°C, and add a few minutes.

Can I air fry vegetables without any oil at all? You can, and they will cook, but they will not brown. Expect a softer, steamed result rather than crisp edges.

Can I cook two different vegetables together? Only if their times are close, like peppers and onions. Otherwise cook them separately and combine afterward.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Whole Chicken: Time, Temperature and Doneness
entry.summary: How to cook a whole chicken in an air fryer, with times by weight, the spatchcock shortcut and the internal temperatures that matter.
entry.content:
A whole roasted chicken is the air fryer's most impressive trick: crisp bronzed skin on all sides in an hour, with the oven free and the kitchen cool. It is also the dish where the machine's limits show — basket size and air flow decide whether you get a roast or a disappointment.

This guide covers the two workable shapes — whole and spatchcocked — with times by weight and the checks that matter. Poultry must reach 165°F / 74°C under USDA rules, and a whole bird has more hiding places for undercooked meat than any cut.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage, basket size and crowding change the clock, but 165°F / 74°C does not change.

First: will your chicken fit?

A 3–4 pound bird fits most 5–6 quart baskets with room to breathe. Anything larger needs the air to circulate around every surface, and it will not if the bird touches the heating element guard or crowds the walls.

Basket sizeWhat fits
3–4 quartSpatchcocked halves only
5–6 quartWhole bird up to 4 lb, or spatchcocked
7 quart and largerWhole bird up to 5 lb

If the bird barely fits, spatchcock it. Removing the backbone and pressing the bird flat cuts the height by half, doubles the skin exposed to hot air, and shortens the cook by a third. Poultry shears make it a two-minute job.

Air fryer whole chicken chart

Roast at a moderate temperature so the breast finishes before the skin burns. Dry the skin thoroughly, oil it lightly and salt it — that trio is what turns into crisp shell.

BirdTemperatureTimeNotes
Whole, 3–4 lb350°F / 177°C50–60 minCheck at 45 min, breast up
Whole, 4–5 lb350°F / 177°C60–70 minTurn once at halfway
Spatchcocked, 3–4 lb380°F / 193°C35–45 minSkin up, no flipping
Spatchcocked, 4–5 lb380°F / 193°C40–50 minCheck the thigh, not the breast

Start checking early. The chart's job is to tell you when to pick up the thermometer, not when to walk away. A whole bird carries heat well and keeps cooking after it leaves the basket, which brings us to the temperatures.

The temperatures that matter in a whole bird

A whole chicken has two meaningful numbers. The breast must reach 165°F / 74°C, the USDA minimum for all poultry. The thigh is better taken higher — its collagen softens as it climbs, and the meat turns tender rather than chalky.

PartTarget internal temperatureWhy
Breast, thickest part165°F / 74°CUSDA minimum for poultry
Thigh, between bone and muscle175°F / 79°C or aboveTender texture, above the minimum
After resting, breastMay rise 5°F / 3°CCarryover during the rest

Probe both places. If the thigh reads 175°F / 79°C and the breast reads 165°F / 74°C, the bird is done everywhere — the breast is the part that cannot be rescued once it overcooks, so verify it first.

Rest the bird 10 minutes under loose foil before carving. The juices that would run onto the board redistribute instead, and the carryover heat finishes the innermost fibers.

Five mistakes with air fryer whole chicken

  1. Buying a bird too big for the basket. No air gap means uneven cooking no matter the time.
  2. Roasting at 400°F / 205°C. The skin burns at the wings before the thigh joint is done.
  3. Skipping the spatchcock on a large bird. Flattening is faster and more even than hoping.
  4. Probing only the breast. The thigh is the slowest spot; check both and let the worse one rule.
  5. Carving immediately. Ten minutes of rest keeps the breast meat juicy instead of pouring its juices out.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a whole chicken take in an air fryer? 50–60 minutes at 350°F / 177°C for a 3–4 pound bird. Spatchcocked, the same bird takes 35–45 minutes at 380°F / 193°C. Always verify with a thermometer at the thigh and breast.

What temperature should the inside of a whole chicken be? 165°F / 74°C minimum in the breast under USDA rules. Take the thigh to 175°F / 79°C or above for the best texture — it stays above the safety floor.

Do I flip the chicken during cooking? For a whole bird, one turn at halfway helps if your basket browns the top more than the bottom. Spatchcocked birds do not need flipping — skin side up the whole time.

Why is my chicken skin soggy underneath? The bird sat in its own rendered fat or the basket was crowded. Dry the skin well before cooking, keep a single bird with air around it, and rest it on a rack after cooking.

Can I cook a partially frozen chicken? No. A whole bird must be fully thawed in the refrigerator — up to 24 hours for a 4 pound bird — before roasting. Partial thawing makes even cooking impossible to verify.

A whole chicken in the air fryer comes down to fit and verification. Give the bird room, flatten it if in doubt, roast at 350°F / 177°C, and let the thermometer — not the clock — call the end.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: How to Clean an Air Fryer (Schedule and Safe Methods)
entry.summary: How to clean an air fryer: a daily, weekly and monthly schedule, dishwasher-safe parts, baked-on grease fixes, element care and odour removal.
entry.content:
Most air fryers die early for one of two reasons: the basket coating gives up, or grease bakes onto the element and starts to smoke. Both are preventable, and both are cleaning problems.

An air fryer is easy to clean if you do it often. The two mistakes people make — soaking the whole appliance and scrubbing with abrasive pads — are exactly the ones that cause damage.

Cleaning guidance varies by appliance model — read your manual before you soak, scrub or dishwasher anything. Wattage and basket size have nothing to do with cleaning, but the finish on your basket decides everything.

Daily, weekly and monthly

Daily is the basket and the drawer. Weekly is the element, the guard and the outer shell. Monthly is the deep clean and an inspection. Do the daily job while the unit is still slightly warm, not hot and not cold, because warm grease wipes away and cold grease has to be chipped.

WhenWhatHow
After every useBasket and crisper plateWarm water, dish soap, soft sponge, dry fully
After every useDrawer cavityWipe with a damp cloth once cool
WeeklyHeating element and guardUnplug and cool, dry soft brush, damp cloth
WeeklyExterior shell and handleDamp cloth, then dry, never wet the vents
MonthlyBaked-on grease on the basketBaking soda paste or vinegar steam
MonthlyRubber seals and element guardInspect for cracking, clean around them
MonthlyCord and plugLook for fraying, heat damage or a loose plug

If you cook greasy food often, treat the weekly row as every two or three uses. A basket of chicken wings leaves far more residue than a basket of toast.

What is dishwasher-safe, and what is not

This is the question with the most wrong answers online, because it depends on your model. There is no universal rule.

  • Check the manual first. Parts listed as dishwasher-safe are usually the basket and the crisper plate, and often only on the top rack.
  • The main unit is never dishwasher-safe. The body contains the fan, the wiring and the element. Water inside it is a shock hazard and a warranty problem.
  • Non-stick coatings vary. Some survive a dishwasher run for years; others lose their release within months. If the manual is silent, wash by hand.
  • Hand washing is always safe. Warm water, a drop of dish soap and a soft sponge works on every model ever made.
  • Dry everything before it goes back. Water left in the drawer rusts the element guard and makes the next cook steam instead of crisp.

Baked-on grease: two methods that work

Baked-on grease is carbonised oil. You cannot wipe it off, and scrubbing it off takes the coating with it. You have to soften it first.

Baking soda paste. Mix three parts baking soda with one part warm water into a paste. Spread it over the stained area, leave it for 15–30 min, then wipe with a soft sponge and warm water. For a stubborn ring, leave it longer rather than pressing harder. Baking soda is a mild abrasive, so use light pressure.

Vinegar steam. Put a bowl of equal parts white vinegar and water in the basket, then run the air fryer at 350°F / 177°C for 8–10 min. The steam loosens the residue on the basket walls. Let everything cool, pour the bowl out, and wipe with a soft sponge. Do not let the bowl run dry, and do not use this method on a unit whose manual warns against heating liquid in the basket.

If neither method moves the stain, stop. A dark, smooth, seasoned patch that does not smell when you heat the unit is cosmetic, not dirty. Chipping at it costs you the non-stick finish, which is a much bigger problem than a stain.

Cleaning the heating element safely

Most air fryers do not have a removable coil. The element sits at the top, above the basket, often behind a metal guard. You clean it in place, and you never submerge it.

  1. Unplug the unit. Not off, unplugged. This is the step people skip.
  2. Let it cool completely. A cool element cannot burn you and clean grease releases better than hot grease.
  3. Turn the unit upside down if the design allows it. On many models the exposed element faces you once the basket is out and the unit is inverted. Check your manual first.
  4. Brush it dry. A soft pastry brush or a dry toothbrush lifts crumbs and flakes off the coil without touching it.
  5. Wipe with a barely damp cloth. Damp, not wet. Clean the coil and the surrounding metal, then dry it immediately.
  6. Never pour or spray water into the cavity. Liquid that reaches the wiring is the single most common way people destroy an air fryer.

If grease is truly baked onto the element and smoking, use a baking soda paste on a cool unit, apply it with a cloth rather than your fingers, leave it 15 min, wipe it off and dry the coil. If the buildup will not come off, and the unit smokes on every use, contact the manufacturer rather than scraping.

Element areaSafe to doNever do
Coil and housingDry brush, barely damp clothSubmerge, spray, soak
Metal guardRemove if the manual allows, wash by handDishwasher if unlisted
Fan and ventWipe the outside onlyPoke anything into the vent
Cord and plugWipe with a dry clothGet wet, pull by the cord

Non-stick care rules for the basket

The coating is the part that decides how long the appliance lasts. Four rules cover it.

  • No metal utensils. Tongs, forks and knives leave scratches that become peeling. Use silicone, wood or plastic.
  • No steel wool or scouring pads. They strip the coating in one session.
  • No oven cleaner. It is designed for bare metal, not coated baskets.
  • No stacking while wet. Baskets stored wet, one inside another, chip each other's coating.

Wash coated parts with a soft sponge and dish soap. If food is stuck, soak in warm soapy water for 10–15 min rather than scraping. If the coating is already flaking into your food, replace the basket or the unit. Flaked coating is not something to cook around.

Odour removal

An air fryer that smells of last week's fish will flavour tonight's dessert. The fix is removal, not covering it up.

  • Vinegar steam. Equal parts vinegar and water in a bowl, 350°F / 177°C for 8–10 min, then wipe and dry.
  • Lemon or citrus peel. Simmer the same way with a few strips of peel for 8–10 min for a fresher smell.
  • Baking soda. Leave an open bowl of dry baking soda in the closed, unplugged unit overnight to absorb stale odours.
  • Wash the seal and the guard. Odour hides in rubber and baked grease, not in the air. If the smell survives a full deep clean, the residue is on the element or the guard.

What voids a warranty

Warranty terms differ by brand. These actions most commonly void coverage — check your manual, because the exact list is model-specific.

  • Submerging the main unit in water or letting liquid run into the housing.
  • Running it in a dishwasher when the manual says hand wash only.
  • Using metal utensils or abrasive cleaners that damage the non-stick coating, since the damage is visible and user-caused.
  • Using oven cleaner, bleach or industrial degreasers on coated parts.
  • Operating it with a damaged cord or plug, or with a bent or dented element guard.
  • Repairing it yourself. Opening the housing generally ends coverage, even if you fix the right part.

Keep the receipt and photograph the rating label on the bottom of the unit. Both make a claim much faster.

Frequently asked questions

How often should I clean my air fryer? The basket after every use, the element and guard weekly, and a full deep clean monthly. Cook greasy food often and you should do the weekly job every two or three uses.

Can I put the air fryer basket in the dishwasher? Only if your manual lists it as dishwasher-safe, and usually only on the top rack. If the manual does not say, hand wash it.

How do I get baked-on grease off an air fryer? Soften it first with a baking soda paste for 15–30 min or a vinegar steam run at 350°F / 177°C for 8–10 min, then wipe with a soft sponge. Do not scrape it.

The short version

Clean the basket daily, the element weekly and the whole unit monthly. Use warm water, dish soap and a soft sponge, and let baking soda or vinegar steam do the work on baked-on grease. Never submerge the main unit, never use metal on the coating, and check your manual before dishwashing anything. Five minutes a week is cheaper than a replacement.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Oven to Air Fryer Conversion Chart (Temperatures and Times)
entry.summary: Convert any oven recipe to an air fryer: lower the temperature about 25°F / 15°C, cut the time about 20 percent, and know when conversion fails.
entry.content:
An air fryer is a small convection oven with the element inches from the food. That proximity is why an oven recipe overcooks in it: same food, same temperature, much more heat where it counts.

The fix is three adjustments. They are rules of thumb, not a formula.

Air fryer models differ in wattage, basket size and how close the element sits to the food. Treat every time below as a range, and verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer.

The three general rules

Rule one: lower the temperature by roughly 25°F / 15°C. Air fryer dials are usually calibrated at the element, not at the food, and the food sits much closer to it.

Rule two: cut the time by roughly 20 percent. A 25–30 min oven step becomes about 20–24 min.

Rule three: check early. Open the basket at about two-thirds of the converted time. Once something is over-browned, there is no way back.

Two constraints matter as much as the numbers. The basket holds one layer, so a sheet-pan recipe becomes two or three rounds. And most air fryers need a 3–5 min preheat for browning.

Oven to air fryer conversion chart

Find your oven temperature, then set the air fryer to the middle column and start at the low end of the time.

Oven temperatureAir fryer temperatureTime changeExample oven time becomes
425°F / 220°C400°F / 205°CCut about 20 percent20–25 min becomes 16–20 min
400°F / 205°C375°F / 190°CCut about 20 percent25–30 min becomes 20–24 min
375°F / 190°C350°F / 177°CCut about 20 percent30–35 min becomes 24–28 min
350°F / 177°C325°F / 163°CCut about 20 percent35–40 min becomes 28–32 min
325°F / 163°C300°F / 149°CCut about 20 percent40–45 min becomes 32–36 min
300°F / 149°C275°F / 135°CCut about 20 percent45–50 min becomes 36–40 min

Read the last column as a starting point. A dense item such as a thick potato needs closer to the original time, while a thin item such as a cookie can be done well before the converted time is up.

What converts well, and what does not

Recipe typeConvertsNotes
Frozen snacks and friesYesUsually better than the oven
Chicken pieces, wings, thighsYesCheck with a thermometer
Small roasts and pork chopsYesMust fit with room around it
Fish fillets and shrimpYesFaster than the chart suggests
Vegetables in 1-inch piecesYesToss in a little oil
Whole chicken or turkeyNoToo tall; the top burns first
Large beef or pork roastsNoWill not fit and will not cook evenly
Wet batters (tempura, fritters)NoBatter drips and burns
Sheet-pan dinnersNoNot enough floor area
Layer cakes and quick breadsNoNeeds a wide, even pan
Soufflés and custardsNoToo delicate for direct hot air
Large pots of soup or stewNoLiquid splashes; nothing browns

When conversion fails, and why

Conversion fails for four reasons, and knowing them saves an inedible batch.

The item is too big. A whole chicken needs even heat over a long time. In a basket, the part closest to the element scorches while the middle climbs.

The coating is wet. Wet batter needs oil at a stable temperature to set the crust, so an air fryer leaves it dripping onto the element. Dry coatings work, such as flour or breadcrumbs.

The pan has to be wide. Cakes, bars, and sheet-pan dinners rely on a flat surface. A round basket cannot reproduce it.

The volume is liquid. Sauces, soups, and stews never reduce in hot air. They evaporate, spatter, and can smoke.

One more failure mode: nothing at all. Some items have no air fryer equivalent, and cooking them elsewhere is not a compromise.

Never invent a conversion for safety

Recipes carry internal temperatures for a reason, and they do not change because the appliance changed.

FoodSafe internal temperature
Chicken and turkey (all parts)165°F / 74°C
Ground meat (beef, pork, lamb)160°F / 71°C
Whole cuts of beef, pork, veal145°F / 63°C + 3 min rest
Fish and shellfish145°F / 63°C
Leftovers, reheated165°F / 74°C

Use an instant-read thermometer on anything thick, stuffed, or bone-in.

Five conversion mistakes

  1. Keeping the oven temperature. The food browns outside before it cooks through.
  2. Keeping the oven time. Twenty percent shorter is the starting point, not a guess.
  3. Overcrowding to save a round. Two layers means steaming, and the food never browns.
  4. Converting a coated recipe. Wet batter will not survive the basket; use a dry coating.
  5. Not checking early. Two minutes late is a burnt batch in a small machine.

Frequently asked questions

Can I convert any oven recipe? Most vegetables, proteins, and frozen foods, yes. Whole birds, large roasts, wet batters, and cakes in wide pans, no.

Why lower the temperature instead of just the time? Because the food sits closer to the element than in a full oven. At the same setting, the outside burns before the inside catches up.

Does the 25°F / 15°C rule scale for a large air fryer? Roughly. Bigger baskets behave more like a small oven, so the gap narrows, but check early and trust the thermometer.

How much oil should I use? Enough for a thin sheen, often about a teaspoon per cup of vegetables. More than that smokes.

What about convection oven recipes? They are already close. Start at the printed temperature, cut the time by about 10 percent, and check early.

The short version

Lower the temperature by roughly 25°F / 15°C, cut the time by roughly 20 percent, and check at two-thirds of the converted time. Convert small, dry-coated foods freely. Skip whole birds, large roasts, wet batters, and anything needing a wide pan.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.
